transcript.text: Hi Rahul, thanks for making the time. I'm on the team hiring for the Manager - Corporate Finance (FP&A and Capital Allocation) role at Varuna Industries Ltd. Over the next 15 minutes or so I'd like to go into your experience, and you'll have time for questions at the end. What is one thing you have learned recently at ISB that has been useful in your work?
transcript.why: This was a warm-up question to help you settle in. It isn't part of the feedback.

transcript.text: yeah sure thank you so much for having me so um one thing I have really picked up at ISB which I found quite useful is actually building a better understanding of financial modeling and scenario analysis like in class we had these hands-on assignments where we had to project cash flows and kind of stress test business assumptions and I realised that in my work earlier uh I was mostly focused on the credit side like assessing borrower risk but now I feel I am more comfortable looking at the whole business holistically like understanding value drivers and not just looking at past numbers so that kind of analytical mindset I would say is really helping me, especially in terms of long-term decision making
Thanks. Walk me through your career so far, with a focus on your credit-risk roles before your MBA.
transcript.why: I moved on after hearing how your recent learning in financial modelling and scenario analysis has influenced the way you view business decisions.

transcript.text: sure so I started my career with Axis Bank right after engineering I joined their credit team handling SME loans so basically I was responsible for preparing credit appraisal notes for small and medium enterprises evaluating their financials business models promoter backgrounds and all I worked on more than 60 proposals there and got a strong foundation about how to analyse various industries understand working capital cycles and so on then after about four years I moved to HDFC Bank in the mid-market corporates division so the borrowers were larger with more complex structures I joined as a credit analyst and then got promoted to senior manager so my primary role was underwriting and monitoring a portfolio of 85 mid-market borrowers with total exposure around 2400 crores it involved end-to-end assessment from initial financial due diligence interacting with relationship managers and risk teams maintaining ongoing client monitoring so for instance tracking early warning signals regular financial health reviews and also mentoring a team of three analysts so that hands-on experience in deeper credit assessment and portfolio management was really the core of my work before I came to ISB
Let’s focus on the stressed auto-components borrower you reviewed at HDFC Bank. What was the hardest part of that review?
transcript.why: Your overview covered your progression, responsibilities, and the scale of your credit work, so I moved to a specific restructuring decision.

transcript.text: yeah so um honestly the hardest part of that review was actually managing a combination of two things like first the information flow from the borrower was quite patchy so their MIS and the monthly numbers weren't coming on time and there were a lot of gaps uh which made it tough to get a clear picture of their cash flows and working capital so we had to keep following up with their CFO and finance team for detailed clarity and secondly since it was a stressed situation everyone including the relationship team and the promoters was a bit tense so aligning everyone while keeping the credit process independent was a challenge and in terms of the actual credit side, um like proposing the restructuring plan I mostly assisted my manager who was leading the discussions with the borrower and the legal team and also bringing in inputs from external consultants so my role was more about compiling the data building the business projections and preparing scenario analysis but finally, all the tough calls on what terms to accept and how to structure it were actually discussed at the credit committee they had the final say so I learned a lot by observing how to handle such sensitive cases especially balancing risk mitigation with keeping the client relationship alive
You described assisting your manager, while the resume says you led the review. What part of the review did you personally own from start to finish?
transcript.why: Your answer described supporting the review, while the resume presents you as leading it, so I asked you to clarify what responsibility was personally yours.

transcript.text: yeah so um actually in terms of the review process itself what I personally owned end-to-end was mainly the financial due diligence and the preparation of all the support documents for the committee so right from collecting all the data from the borrower their financials GST returns bank statements supplier and debtor lists and all, I basically drove that part myself I was also the one who built the cash flow projections under different stress scenarios and analysed what kind of restructuring could work given their actual cash generation I coordinated with the borrower CFO and their consultants directly for clarification, and I also had to answer a lot of follow-ups from both our risk and legal teams on the numbers and assumptions so basically all the groundwork—the analysis pack, projections, sensitivity checks and putting the initial proposal together for my manager and then for the committee—that was completely under my ownership but yeah for the final structuring terms and negotiation with the borrower, my manager was the front face leading those parts, and the decisions were taken in the committee, but all the numbers and options prepared for the committee were from my side
You owned the diligence, projections, and proposal materials. How was it determined that the restructuring avoided an NPA classification?
transcript.why: You clarified which parts of the review you personally owned, but not how the stated avoidance of an NPA classification was established. I asked how that outcome was determined.

transcript.text: yeah so actually once we put together the restructuring proposal like we had to submit detailed cash flow analysis projections for at least two years with all the assumptions justified and based on the RBI guidelines at that time like if the proposal’s implementation meets certain conditions within a specified timeline then the account doesn't slip into NPA so in our case after the proposal was approved by the credit committee it went for implementation and the borrower complied with the conditions like bringing in additional collateral and fresh capital from promoters within the 30-day period, so as per the RBI circular, if these steps are done on time, the status remains standard and it doesn’t get classified as NPA the borrower also regularised their overdue repayments as per restructured terms so the monitoring team basically checked all the compliance, reviewed the documentation and confirmed that the account met all criteria on time and the regular monitoring continued so that’s how it was officially categorised as a standard asset and not NPA I mostly supported the documentation and monitoring process here but the compliance review was mainly done by our monitoring and policy teams
Understood. At Axis Bank, what did you have to figure out first when preparing a credit appraisal note for a new SME proposal?
transcript.why: You explained how the account’s status was determined and who confirmed that the conditions were met. I’m moving to a different credit appraisal example to understand how you approached individual proposals earlier in your career.

transcript.text: so um actually the very first thing I had to figure out whenever I got a new SME proposal was to really understand the business model like what exactly the company does who are their main customers and suppliers how does their revenue cycle work and basically what is the end-to-end value chain because only after understanding this you can make sense of their financials you know so I would usually first talk to the relationship manager to get some background then dig into the last three year financial statements to check for revenue consistency seasonality margins and so on and also look at their working capital cycle like how much is locked in receivables and inventory versus payables and then of course understand the promoter profile what's their background repayment track record and any group exposures so yeah for me the foundation always had to be a clear picture of what drives the business and how stable or risky it is before I start looking deeper into ratios and cash flows and preparing the final credit note
Which decisions or sections of the appraisal note were specifically yours to prepare or recommend?
transcript.why: Your answer described the appraisal process and the steps you took, but not yet which part was specifically yours within the broader team process. I asked you to clarify your personal contribution.

transcript.text: yeah so in Axis Bank the appraisal note was kind of divided into different sections and as the credit analyst it was my responsibility to prepare and recommend most of the credit part so for example, the assessment of the borrower’s business background financial analysis working capital assessment and actually all the ratio analysis projections were entirely done by me like I had to arrive at things like what is the right working capital limit required or if any enhancement is justified based on sales trends and business growth so those recommendations I had to defend in front of my manager then I would also propose draft terms and covenants like DSCR minimum, collateral cover LTV etc like I would put my recommendation but the legal and compliance sections were prepared by other teams so basically all the numbers and main credit call part I had to prepare and recommend but final approval and sanctioning always happened at a higher level
Take one SME proposal where your analysis affected the credit recommendation. What was the first analysis you performed on that case?
transcript.why: You described the sections you owned, but not one specific proposal showing how you applied that analysis. I asked you to walk through the steps on a concrete case.

transcript.text: yeah sure so um one specific proposal I remember was for this engineering parts manufacturer who were applying for an enhancement in their working capital limits so the very first analysis I performed there was actually a trend analysis of their sales and receivables over the past three years like I wanted to see if their sales growth was consistent with what they were projecting and whether the increase in receivables was justified or pointing to any stress I pulled out their audited financials and also looked at the debtor ageing report to check if any major portion was stuck with one buyer or if there were old outstanding amounts so this analysis kind of set the tone because I saw that while the topline was rising sharply, the receivables were growing at a faster pace and a lot of dues were actually overdue so that flagged a possible risk to cash flows I highlighted this to my manager right up front and then in the rest of the note, I recommended a lower limit than what was applied and suggested tighter monitoring on collections so basically the first thing was establishing whether their growth narrative matched the on-ground cash realisation and then all other analysis kind of built on that insight
How would you assess a proposal for a new production line at Varuna when the business case depends on uncertain demand?
transcript.why: Your example showed what you personally analysed and how it changed the recommendation, so I moved to a capital-allocation scenario relevant to the role.

transcript.text: so um if I had to assess a proposal for a new production line at Varuna and the business case had uncertain demand I think the first thing would be to actually break down the demand assumptions and see how realistic and data-driven they are like whether they are based on actual market studies customer commitments or just internal optimism so I would want to see if there are any anchor clients already on board or long-term agreements or if it is mostly projected uptake then I would probably build out a few scenario models like best case, base case, and worst case for demand and map out how those would impact cash flows and return metrics and see at what level does the project start making sense or hit breakeven I would also look at competitive landscape and whether there is risk of pricing pressure or overcapacity in the sector then the other thing would be to check flexibility like is it possible to ramp up or down production if demand deviates so risks to fixed costs become a big issue also I’d stress test the funding structure to ensure that even in a low-demand scenario, the company can still manage debt covenants and liquidity so basically a lot would depend on the quality of demand-side validation and then continuous monitoring if the proposal moves ahead, so that the business isn’t exposed to one single bet on untested demand
Let’s switch to fit. You are moving from credit risk into corporate finance. What draws you to the Manager role at Varuna Industries?
transcript.why: Your answer explained how you would validate demand, model different outcomes, and protect the company from downside funding and capacity risk.

transcript.text: yeah so actually for me the main excitement about this role at Varuna is that it’s a genuine step towards seeing the business side from a broader angle rather than just from a lender’s risk lens like in credit risk, I was always analysing financials and business models but mostly as an outsider with a focus on risk containment whereas in corporate finance especially FP&A and capital allocation you get to drive decisions that directly shape the growth and performance of the business so that’s really the direction I want to move in and Varuna is an interesting place because you guys are at that stage where capital decisions really matter, whether it’s new product lines or managing funding mix, and I feel my analytical background plus my exposure to many different industries can be useful in evaluating investments and resource allocation here I’ve also realised during my time at ISB and working on some finance projects that I really enjoy the challenge of making business choices under uncertainty rather than just pointing out risks and stepping back so this manager role seems like the perfect next step to put all that together and actually help drive strategy from inside

Manager - Corporate Finance (FP&A and Capital Allocation)
Varuna Industries Ltd, Pune

Varuna Industries is a listed auto-components manufacturer (revenue INR 6,500 crore) with 14 plants in India.

Role
- Own the annual operating plan and monthly business reviews for two business units
- Evaluate capex proposals (new lines, capacity expansion) and present recommendations to the CFO
- Work with treasury on working-capital and debt decisions
- Lead a team of 2 analysts

Must have
- 5+ years in corporate finance, credit or investment banking
- Strong financial modelling and capital-budgeting skills
- Stakeholder management with plant and business heads

topics.jd_line: Strong financial modelling and capital-budgeting skills
topics.question: How would you assess a proposal for a new production line at Varuna when the business case depends on uncertain demand?
answer_plan: Validate demand using customer commitments, market evidence, and the competitive landscape.
Build best-case, base-case, and worst-case cash-flow models with return and breakeven measures.
Stress-test capacity flexibility, debt covenants, and liquidity under the downside case.
Recommend approval, rejection, or staged investment with clear monitoring conditions.
topics.example_answer: I would first validate the demand assumptions using customer commitments, market data, and the risk of pricing pressure or overcapacity. Then I would model best-case, base-case, and downside cash flows, including capex, working capital, operating costs, returns, and breakeven. I would test whether the line can be added in stages and whether the downside case still protects liquidity and debt capacity. I would recommend approval only if the base case meets the return requirement and the downside case remains manageable, with monitoring triggers after launch.

ratings.reason: You correctly covered demand validation, cash-flow scenarios, return metrics, production flexibility, debt covenants, and liquidity.
